news.author: Piero Cingari
news.content:
The artificial intelligence trade broke down for a third consecutive week, and the damage this time came straight from the balance sheets of the companies funding the buildout.

Two weeks ago, investors worried about valuations. Last week, they asked who would pay the bill. This week, Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) , Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC) handed them the invoice.

By Friday afternoon, the Nasdaq 100 had slid about 4% on the session to its lowest level since early August and was down roughly 2.5% for the week, its third straight weekly decline. The S&P 500 was off about 2% on the day and close to 1% on the week.

• Alphabet stock is facing resistance. Why are GOOG shares declining?

Alphabet’s Worst Week In 15 Years

Alphabet Inc. lit the fuse on Wednesday night. Revenue came in short of expectations, free cash flow swung to a roughly $9 billion outflow, and management signaled that capital spending will climb again in 2027.

Thursday’s 13% drop was the steepest single-session decline in the stock’s history and erased roughly $482 billion of market value. Shares are down about 13% for the week, the worst weekly showing since August 2011.

The pain spread across the sector. The Communication Services Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLC) is on track for an eighth straight daily loss, its longest losing streak since the fund launched in 2018.

Amazon added to the pressure Thursday night. Earnings of $1.89 per share fell short of the $1.96 consensus, while the company said 2027 capital expenditures will be “meaningfully more” than this year’s roughly $220 billion.

Read Also: Alphabet Sinks 11.8%, Small Caps Rally on Strong GDP Growth: Stock Market Today

Intel’s Worst Day Ever

Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC) delivered the week’s most violent move. The chipmaker guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, well below the $17.07 billion analysts expected, and said it does not expect positive cash flow this year as PC demand weakens.

Shares collapsed about 30% on Friday, the worst session in Intel’s trading history, with no comparable decline in more than 11,700 sessions since 1980.

Bank of America Global Research downgraded the stock to Neutral from Buy, saying in a Friday report that the agentic server CPU tide “is more than offset by PC/supply headwinds.”

Chart: Intel Plunged 30%, Surpassing July 1974’s Drop

Read Also: Chip Stocks Lose $1 Trillion as Intel Sinks 28%

Warsh: ‘Interest Rates Get In The Cracks’

The Federal Reserve left the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday. The decision passed 10-2, with Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissenting in favor of a quarter-point hike.

Chair Kevin Warsh declined to commit to a December move.

“I don’t believe in forward guidance absent exigent circumstances,” he said.

Asked whether higher borrowing costs could cool the AI boom, he offered a line that aged quickly over the next 48 hours.

“Interest rates get in the cracks. Interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything,” Warsh said.

He indicated that investors have grown more selective about where they put money, noting that credit spreads on some assets have blown out while financial conditions have tightened for others.

Thursday’s data gave both camps ammunition.

Third-quarter GDP expanded at a 3.4% annualized pace, ahead of the 3.2% forecast, while the PCE price index accelerated to 3.6% year over year from 3.4%. Weekly jobless claims slipped to 194,000, below the 199,000 expected.

CME FedWatch now prices a 74% probability of a December rate hike, down from 85% right after Wednesday’s meeting.

Treasuries Catch A Bid

Bonds became the safe harbor. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to about 4.92%, after touching 4.89% earlier in the day, the lowest since early September. The 2-year yield dropped to 4.57% and the 30-year held near 5.31%.

Health Care’s Best Month Ever Against the Market

As money fled technology, defensive sectors absorbed it.

The Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLV) is on track for its best month ever relative to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY), outperforming by 11% in October, according to data going back to 1998. The previous record was March 2020, at 9.9%.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (NASDAQ:IBB) climbed to an all-time high this week. Regeneron Pharmaceuticals Inc. (NASDAQ:REGN) surged 11% on Friday, its best day since October 2025.

Best and Worst S&P 500 Stocks This Week

The top performers in the S&P 500 this week were Carvana Co. (NYSE:CVNA), up nearly 20%; Pentair plc (NYSE:PNR), up 19.6%, and Vertiv Holdings Co. (NYSE:VRT), up 18%.

At the bottom, Reddit Inc. (NYSE:RDDT) lost about 38% after CEO Steve Huffman warned daily active visitors could fall by a low double-digit percentage in the fourth quarter.

ServiceNow Inc. (NYSE:NOW) dropped nearly 35% after its quarterly report, and Intel fell close to 27%.

Reddit’s 30% plunge on Friday was also the worst day in its history and stretched its losing run to eight sessions, a 41.9% slide.

Records and Streaks

Several stocks are writing history.

Albemarle Corp. (NYSE:ALB) is on track for a 10th straight weekly loss, down 36.9% over the stretch, the longest losing streak in data going back to 1994. The previous record was nine weeks in March 2000.

Interactive Brokers Group Inc. (NASDAQ:IBKR) is heading for a ninth straight weekly drop, a 20.5% decline that doubles as a new record, while SanDisk Corp. (NASDAQ:SNDK) has fallen six weeks in a row, losing 36.6%.

Boeing Co. (NYSE:BA) is down eight weeks in a row, its longest losing stretch since October 2023, and Robinhood Markets Inc. (NASDAQ:HOOD) is on a six-week slide of 30.7%.

On the upside, Marathon Petroleum Corp. (NYSE:MPC) is set for a 10th straight monthly gain, up 171%, matching its record from March 2013. HCA Healthcare Inc. (NYSE:HCA) has risen five months in a row, tying its March 2024 record, and Marriott International Inc. (NASDAQ:MAR) is up seven straight weeks.

Among Friday’s other movers, FedEx Freight Holding Co. (NASDAQ:FDXF) jumped 16%, its best day since May, and Global Payments Inc. (NYSE:GPN) rose 10%. Illumina Inc. (NASDAQ:ILMN) dropped 19%, its worst session since October 2016.

Detroit Rides The Rotation

General Motors Co. (NYSE:GM) gained about 15% this week, its best weekly performance since October 2025. The stock rallied 5.5% on Tuesday after GM announced it will move its listing to Nasdaq on Nov. 17 and invest in its Lansing Delta Township plant to build hybrid vehicles.

Ford Motor Co. (NYSE:F) added about 5% after third-quarter results topped expectations. Revenue reached $49.53 billion against a $46.24 billion estimate, and adjusted EPS of 49 cents beat the 41-cent consensus. Ford also lifted the bottom of its full-year adjusted EBIT guidance to $10.5 billion.

“Ford delivered a strong quarter as we’re entering a defining phase of the company’s transformation,” CEO Jim Farley said.

See More: Top Momentum Stocks

What’s Next: Apple, Midterms and Jobs

Next week brings no Fed meeting, but it does test whether the AI sell-off can find a floor.

Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) and Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR) report Monday after the close. Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) and Super Micro Computer Inc. (NASDAQ:SMCI) follow on Tuesday, the same day Americans vote in the midterm elections. Qualcomm Inc. (NASDAQ:QCOM) and Arm Holdings plc (NASDAQ:ARM) report Wednesday.

The week closes with the October jobs report on Friday, Nov. 6, the last payrolls print before the Fed’s December decision. After September’s 29,000 gain, traders will be watching for any sign the labor market is softening enough to take a December hike off the table.

news.author: Mohd Haider
news.content:
S&P Global Ratings (NYSE:SPGI) revised its outlook on Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) to "negative" from "stable" on Friday, citing uncertainty over the company’s capital spending and free operating cash flow (FOCF).

Spending Plans Raise Red Flags

Last week, Meta forecast annual capital expenditure of $135 billion to $145 billion. It also posted a third-quarter free cash flow deficit of $2.12 billion. The company plans to sell $97.5 billion in stock to fund its AI investments.

S&P now expects Meta’s FOCF deficits of $22 billion in 2026 and $71 billion in 2027, and lessening losses in 2028, about $39 billion.

S&P said, "we are less certain that it will curtail its spending as previously anticipated."

Leverage Could Test ‘AA-’ Rating Threshold

S&P said Meta’s leverage could top 1.0x as early as 2027. That is the downgrade threshold for its "AA-" issuer credit rating. Leverage rose from 0.1x in 2025, mainly because Meta leases data-center capacity rather than issuing debt, S&P said.

Long-term debt stood at $80.92 billion as of Sept. 30.

In mid-October, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said its profitable core business and strong credit let it underwrite AI costs. He said other tech companies would pay for Meta’s computing capacity if its AI products fail, but the technology succeeds broadly.

Some market participants also disagree with S&P’s caution. Aptus Capital Advisors portfolio manager David Wagner said worries over Meta’s debt and AI spending look overstated, because hyperscalers carry much stronger debt coverage than the broader market.

AI Spending Draws Wider Credit Scrutiny

Earlier this year, S&P cut Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL) to ‘BBB-/A-3’ from ‘BBB/A-2’

Meta has a market capitalization of $1.572 trillion, a 52-week high of $779.82 and a 52-week low of $520.26.

news.author: Ananya Gairola
news.content:
Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) has renewed her criticism of the Donald Trump administration’s approach to artificial intelligence (AI) regulation, arguing that voluntary safety commitments from major tech companies are no substitute for enforceable government oversight.

Warren Slams Trump’s Voluntary AI Safety Agreement

On Friday, Warren took to X to accuse Republicans of failing to establish meaningful safeguards for the rapidly developing AI industry.

She questioned whether Trump’s meeting with leading AI executives had influenced the administration’s preference for industry-led oversight, suggesting that companies had effectively been allowed to regulate themselves.

“Republicans in charge of Congress are not lifting a finger to regulate AI,” Warren wrote. She added, "Why? Maybe because Trump had a nice dinner with the AI CEOs and they decided "tremendous self-regulation" is good enough to keep us safe."

“It’s a recipe for disaster,” Warren warned.

In September, Trump hosted executives from companies including OpenAI, Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META), Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Anthropic, unveiling the voluntary White House Accord on Super Intelligence.

The agreement encourages AI companies to strengthen internal safeguards, conduct independent audits and establish board-level oversight.

Trump described the commitments as “morally binding.”

Read Also: Sam Altman Breaks With Anthropic on AI Regulation, Says World Must Accept ‘Some Bad Things’ as AI Benefits Outweigh Harms

Warren Raises Concerns Over Anthropic’s $2 Trillion IPO

Warren’s latest criticism comes just days after The Wall Street Journal reported that she had demanded answers from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about risks disclosed in the company’s initial public offering (IPO) paperwork.

In a letter sent Tuesday, Warren said the potential dangers of Anthropic’s technology “demand greater scrutiny” before the company becomes further intertwined with public financial markets.

Her four-page letter included questions about existential AI risks, public safety, partnerships with Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO), and how Anthropic intends to justify a potential valuation approaching $2 trillion.

She requested “exhaustive responses” by Nov. 3.

Former White House Adviser Defends Industry-Led AI Oversight

Earlier, Former Trump adviser David Sacks has defended the voluntary agreement, arguing that independent audits, board accountability and existing federal laws could give it meaningful enforcement power.

He has also argued that the framework could avoid the delays and unintended consequences of establishing a new AI regulatory agency.

However, Warren, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) have questioned whether voluntary commitments can adequately protect the public from risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems.

news.author: Mohd Haider
news.content:
Venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya warned that AI companies’ debt has reached an estimated $340 billion to $400 billion, threatening to crowd out U.S. Treasury demand, as seven or eight firms drive a massive spending push.

Cash-Rich Tech Giants Shift Into AI ‘Spending Binge’ Mode

Speaking on the All In podcast episode that aired on Friday, Palihapitiya said "seven or eight companies" now set the tone for the entire country.

“The entire United States economy is levered to the AI complex,” said Palihapitiya.

The Sri Lankan-born Canadian-American tech commentator said these firms were once highly profitable and cash-generative. They are now in what he called a "massive spending binge" on AI.

The warning comes as the spending strains balance sheets. S&P Global Ratings (NYSE:SPGI) cut its outlook on Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) to negative on Friday, citing uncertain capital spending and cash flow.

Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) reported negative free cash flow, meaning it spent more than it generated.

Big Tech Debt Surges as AI Spending Drains Cash

Palihapitiya said the heavy spending is draining cash, forcing the companies to raise debt.

Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) was the exception, he said. He credited CEO Satya Nadella with halving the company’s debt while peers borrowed far more.

Microsoft’s latest results show how the spending debate is playing out. Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives called the company a "barometer" for AI spending. Azure, its cloud platform, grew 48% year over year, beating expectations of about 45%.

Markets are noticing. Bloomberg Tech host Ed Ludlow said "Wall Street cares about free cash flow now," as investors grow less tolerant of cash-hungry AI spending.

Treasury Market Crowd-Out Risk for Investors

During the podcast, the bigger concern, Palihapitiya said, is "crowding out." That happens when heavy borrowing by one group absorbs investor money that would otherwise go elsewhere.

He said AI firms’ funding needs through the end of 2027 equal about 30% of expected U.S. Treasury issuance over the same period. Treasuries are debt securities sold by the federal government. In his view, the companies will compete with them for investor demand.

The strain is already visible. OpenAI reportedly cut its latest fundraising target by $10 billion to about $20 billion amid a tech selloff driven by AI spending worries.

The S&P 500 Index pulled back to 7,530 on Friday, its lowest level since September 16 and 4% below its all-time high. It had earlier hit a major barrier at 7,830 as AI jitters spread, even as corporate earnings gained momentum and its forward price-to-earnings ratio dropped.

US Stocks are Falling as the Earnings Season Escalates

The S&P 500 Index has come under pressure in the past few weeks as investors have dumped the top companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry. 

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), the biggest company in the index, dropped to $201, down by 17.2% from the year-to-date high. Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) dropped to $278, down by 31% from its all-time high.

Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) fell to a low of $229 from the year-to-date high of $287. A closer look shows that most S&P 500 constituents have dropped by double digits from their highest points this year. This includes companies in the technology, retail, financial services, and consumer industries. 

Read Also: Coinbase, Robinhood and Other Crypto Exchange Stocks Tumble as Binance Hack Exposes Vulnerabilities

The S&P 500’s retreat has coincided with a relatively strong earnings season. FactSet (NYSE:FDS) data shows that 60% of companies in the index have reported results, with blended earnings growth of 30%, above the 29% analysts expected.

The strong earnings growth has also coincided with the falling valuation, with its forward price-to-earnings ratio being 18.7, well below the five-year average of 19.8. This multiple is also below the ten-year average of 19.1.

The next important catalyst for the S&P 500 Index and its ETFs like VOO, SPY, and IVV will be more earnings from top companies. Some of the top companies to watch will be Apple, Palantir, AMD, Amgen, Arm Holdings, McDonald’s, and ConocoPhillips. 

US Stocks are Falling Amid AI Jitters

The ongoing retreat of the US stock market has coincided with the AI jitters, which escalated this week. Top companies like Intel, Amazon, and Google dropped as concerns about the AI industry continued. Amazon and Google dropped after committing to keep their capital spending and after their earnings showed that core revenue was slowing. 

There have been some notable negative AI news. For example, OpenAI has raised just $11 billion, well short of its $30 billion target. Also, Anthropic’s S1 document showed that it made over $80 billion in losses. Bond yields of top companies like Oracle and CoreWeave have continued soaring. 

The AI Stock Index has jumped to 74, while some top analysts like Ray Dalio and Ken Griffin have warned that the bubble may burst soon. 

S&P 500 Index Has Hit a Crucial Barrier

SPX chart | Source: TradingView

On the charts, the daily chart shows that the SPX Index has hit a crucial resistance level of 7,813. It formed a double-top pattern whose neckline is at 7,507, its lowest swing in September. 

The index has already dropped below the 50-day moving average, a sign that bears remain in control. Therefore, the most likely scenario is where it continues falling, potentially to the 38.2% Fibonacci Retracement level of 7,261, down by 4.2% from the current level.

news.author: Crispus Nyaga
news.content:
Anthropic, the creator of the popular AI chatbot Claude, is preparing for an initial public offering (IPO) that could come as soon as November. The listing faces some major headwinds, however, as concerns about the artificial intelligence industry persist.

Anthropic IPO Comes as AI Companies Plunge

Anthropic’s upcoming IPO comes at a time when most AI stocks have plunged. In Hong Kong, shares of Z.ai and MiniMax have dropped more than 80% from their all-time highs. Both companies are comparable to Anthropic because their businesses focus on building AI models.

The same trend is happening in the United States, where top AI companies are falling. This includes popular names like Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Micron (NASDAQ:MU), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG), and SanDisk (NASDAQ:SNDK).

Most importantly, SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX), which went public in June, has slumped by 40% from its peak, erasing billions of dollars in value. SpaceX is a big player in the AI space, thanks to its ownership of Grok and its data center leasing business.

Therefore, there is a risk that Anthropic’s stock will also drop, especially if the IPO happens in this environment. Indeed, most Polymarket traders see the company’s valuation at $1.5 trillion in December. 

Read Also: Peter Schiff Says a Monday Stock Market Crash Could Boost Democrats' Chances of Taking Senate as Party's Victory Odds Hit 71%: Both Republicans and Democrats Have to ‘Lie’ About the Economy

Historically, companies tend to list when the markets are booming as that normally increases the value of their shares. SpaceX’s IPO in June happened as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 indices were hovering near their all-time highs. 

Investors are Pushing Back Against AI Valuations

Anthropic’s IPO is also coming as investors continue pushing back against the hefty AI valuations. For example, Firmus, an Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) backed data center company, recently ended its IPO process as investors pushed back against the $30 billion valuation.

Nscale, another Nvidia-backed data center company, is considering slashing its hefty $33 billion valuation as investors push back. Besides, shares of other top neocloud companies like CoreWeave, Nebius, and IREN have all plunged. 

Concerns of Anthropic’s valuation rose after it published its prospectus, which revealed the magnitude of its spending. It made $16.8 billion in revenue in the year’s first half, but lost $80 billion. The company plans to keep spending in the coming years. 

At the same time, Blackstone (NYSE:BX) has warned that the company may struggle to get an investment-grade rating after its IPO. Such a move will dramatically raise its borrowing costs over time. 

In another sign that investors are pushing back, OpenAI raised $11 billion from investors, much lower than the $30 billion it was seeking. 

As such, there is a real risk that the company may decide to pause its IPO until market conditions improve.

news.author: Crispus Nyaga
news.content:
OpenAI, the artificial intelligence (AI) pioneer, is facing headwinds as its revenue growth slows, its cash burn climbs, and its fundraising hits a roadblock. These pressures come amid persistent fears that the AI bubble is about to burst.

OpenAI Raised Just $11 Billion at a $1.25 Trillion Valuation

OpenAI’s latest fundraising fell short of its target, a sign that investors are questioning its valuation as evidence mounts that its business is decelerating. The company raised $11.5 billion, lifting its valuation to $1.25 trillion, well below the $1.4 trillion it was targeting. By contrast, Anthropic is eyeing a $2 trillion valuation in its IPO.

OpenAI’s fundraising comes at a difficult time for the company. Its cash burn is continuing, with estimates showing it will incinerate more than $280 billion through 2030. At the same time, its annualized revenue is below $50 billion, short of the $70 billion analysts were expecting. Competition from Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) and open-weight models like DeepSeek and Kimi has also intensified.

Read Also: A SpaceX and Tesla Merger Would Build a Conglomerate Just as Spin-Offs Thrive

OpenAI has also delayed its IPO from this year to 2027. While management has cited AI safety concerns, the reality is that it is worried about its fundamentals. It fears that, as things stand, a listing would likely trigger a sharp selloff in its stock.

The fundraising also comes at a time when investors are pushing back against AI valuations. Firmus, an Australian company, recently pulled its IPO as investors pushed back against its valuation. Most AI companies, including hyperscalers like Alphabet, Meta Platforms, and Amazon, have all plunged in the past few weeks.

At the same time, some popular figures have warned about the AI bubble. These include Citadel’s Ken Griffin and Bridgewater Associates’ Ray Dalio.

ChatGPT has Lost Market Share

The fundraising also comes at a time when ChatGPT’s market share has continued falling this year. Its share dropped below 50% for the first time ever. Since then, other companies have continued to gain share in the US and internationally. 

Anthropic’s Claude has become one of the fastest-growing players in the industry. In its S1, the company said that its revenue soared to over $16.8 billion in the first half of the year from $1.6 billion in the same period last year. Moonshot’s Kimi, Google’s Gemini, and Meta’s Muse have also grown. 

OpenAI is taking actions to boost its business ahead of its IPO. It has slashed prices of its models, introduced advertising, and released more advanced models.

news.author: Crispus Nyaga
news.content:
Top memory stocks like Micron (NASDAQ:MU), SanDisk (NASDAQ:SNDK), and Western Digital (NASDAQ:WDC) extended their decline as investors exited artificial intelligence positions.

Micron, the third-largest player in the high-bandwidth memory market, fell for a fifth consecutive week, ending at $884, 30% below its year-to-date high. SanDisk and Western Digital have dropped 51% and 54%, respectively. The Roundhill Memory ETF (CBOE: DRAM) fell to $48, 41% below its year-to-date high.

Memory Stocks Have Slumped as AI Slowdown Remains

Memory companies like Micron, SanDisk, and Western Digital have fallen in the past few months as investors remain concerned about the AI sector. 

Investors are concerned that the AI sector is starting to slow down, which will impact demand for memory products. One reason for this is the elevated interest rates and bond yields. In a statement this week, Elon Musk warned that over 200 neocloud companies will collapse as funding dries. 

There are signs that the funding issues are affecting the biggest companies. OpenAI, the AI pioneer, is concluding its fundraising, taking in $11 billion, well below its target of $30 billion. It has also lowered its target valuation from $1.4 trillion to $1.25 trillion.

Top spenders in the AI space, including hyperscalers like Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META), and Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG), have come under pressure as investors question their massive capital expenditures. Most of these companies are now reporting negative free cash flow. 

As such, there is fear that a slowdown in AI spending by hyperscalers and other companies in the industry will lead to weak demand for memory products. At the same time, there are concerns that competition from Chinese companies like CXMT will put pressure on memory prices. 

Read Also: Coinbase, Robinhood and Other Crypto Exchange Stocks Tumble as Binance Hack Exposes Vulnerabilities

Micron, SanDisk, Western Digital, and other Memory Companies Have Catalysts

On the positive side, there are several potential catalysts that may drive memory companies higher. One of them is that their revenue growth and profits are accelerating. SanDisk said that its revenue rose by 378% YoY in the September quarter to $11 billion, with its net income rising to $8 billion. 

Similarly, Western Digital said that its revenue jumped by 55% to $4.38 billion. In South Korea, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix also published strong numbers. All these companies said that demand was still strong and that they were sold out for the coming year. 

Further, these companies are returning cash to their investors. SanDisk returned $5 billion to shareholders in the quarter. It has repurchased 4% of its outstanding shares in the last two quarters. Western Digital continued its buyback and hiked its dividends by 17%.

Micron has said that it will repurchase shares worth $35 billion starting in December when the CHIPS Act restrictions end. Other companies like Samsung and SK Hynix are returning billions of dollars to their shareholders.

All of this is happening as they have become some of the cheapest companies on Wall Street. SanDisk has a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 5, while Micron and Western Digital trade at multiples of 5.02 and 14.8, respectively. By contrast, the S&P 500 Index trades at a forward multiple of 18.6. As such, bargain hunters could start buying the dip.
